# Homework overview

The COVID-19 pandemic made a familiar public-health instruction suddenly global: wash your hands. Hand washing only works if people have water they can use and somewhere safe to manage human waste. Clean water and sanitation are therefore not only development goals; they are infrastructure that determines whether simple interventions can succeed.

Using a 2020 update published by [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/water-sanitation-2020-update), we will look at how access to water and sanitation changed around the world between 2000 and 2020. Death and illness from preventable infections remain far more common in places where that infrastructure is missing.

```{marginfigure}
More background on the indicators and service-level definitions is on the [Our World in Data sanitation page](https://ourworldindata.org/sanitation).
```

## Learning goals

By the end of this homework, you should be able to:

A. Report a number from data with inline R code rather than typing the digit by hand.
B. Filter, arrange, and summarize rows with `dplyr`.
C. Build faceted histograms and scatterplots in `ggplot2`.
D. Compare water and sanitation access across countries and years.
E. Make a simple time-series plot and interpret rates of change.

# Packages and data

We will use the **tidyverse** for wrangling and visualization. The package is already installed. Load it, then read the data from the `data` folder of your repository.

```{r load-packages-data-demo, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
wat_san <- read_csv("data/water-and-sanitation.csv")
```

## Viewing the data

You can inspect the data frame as a spreadsheet with `View(wat_san)`. Type that command in the **Console**, not in your R Markdown file. `View()` opens an interactive window, which does not belong in a static knitted document.

This is a custom course dataset, so `?wat_san` will not open a help file. Use the variable list below instead.

Each column is a variable. You can print the names with:

```{r names-demo}
names(wat_san)
```

- `Entity`: Country name, or a regional / income-group aggregate, or `World`
- `Year`: Year of the estimate
- `water_*`: Percent of the population at a given water-service level
- `sanitation_*`: Percent of the population at a given sanitation-service level

Suffixes added to `water_` or `sanitation_`:

- `_improved`: Improved access (safely managed, basic, or limited)
- `_safe`: Safely managed (for sanitation: a private, hygienic toilet whose waste is treated)
- `_basic`: Basic improved service
- `_limited`: Limited improved service (for sanitation: a shared toilet)
- `_unimproved`: Unimproved facility (for sanitation: often a poorly maintained pit latrine)
- `_none`: No service (for sanitation: open defecation; for water: no improved source)

## Exercise 3 — Open defecation over time

**Goal:** Compare a numerical distribution across years with a faceted histogram.

Create a faceted histogram in which each facet is a year and the plotted variable is the percent of the population with **no sanitation service** (`sanitation_none`).

- Does it look as if rates of open defecation have changed between 2000 and 2020?
- What features of the distributions have changed over time, if any?

A skeleton is already in your starter file. Fill in the blanks.

```{r no-sanitation-years-demo, echo = TRUE}
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = ___) +
  facet_wrap(~___)
```

How to read that skeleton:

- `ggplot()` starts the plot.
- The first layer names the data frame and maps variables to **aes**thetics (here, the x-axis).
- `geom_histogram()` displays the distribution. Try a few bin widths and keep one that makes the year-to-year comparison readable.
- `facet_wrap()` splits the plot into panels. Facet by **year**, not by entity.

### Exercise 3 checkpoint

## Exercise 4 — Highest “no sanitation” rates in 2000

**Goal:** Filter a year, then sort or slice to find the most extreme countries.

In a single pipeline, identify the entities with the highest rates of no sanitation service in **2000** and arrange them in descending order.

```{marginfigure}
**Hint:** `slice_max()` from week 1 is a compact way to keep the largest values of a variable. Run `?slice_max` if you need the arguments.
```

A pipeline shaped like `data %>% filter() %>% arrange()` or `data %>% filter() %>% slice_max()` is enough. Looking at five to ten rows is plenty.

- Compare the `water_none` and `sanitation_none` columns in the output.
- Do water and sanitation infrastructure appear tightly associated in these rows, or not?

## Exercise 7 — Summarize 2000 vs. 2020

**Goal:** Use `group_by()` and `summarize()` to compare the distribution of `water_none` and `sanitation_none` in two years.

Calculate the minimum, mean, median, standard deviation, IQR, and maximum of `water_none` and `sanitation_none` in **2000** and **2020**.

- Filter to those two years and drop the `Entity` value `"World"` so that the World aggregate is not mixed into the country-level summaries. Regional aggregates may still be present; that is acceptable.
- What do you notice about the values between 2000 and 2020?
- What do you notice when you compare the sanitation summaries with the water summaries?

```{marginfigure}
The filter line combines `==`, `!=`, `&`, and `|`. Because `&` is evaluated before `|`, the provided pattern keeps 2000-not-World **or** 2020-not-World. `Year %in% c(2000, 2020) & Entity != "World"` does the same job in one condition if you prefer it.
```

```{r progress-summary-demo, echo = TRUE}
wat_san %>% 
  filter(Year == ___ & Entity != "World" | Year == ___ & Entity != "World") %>% 
  group_by(Year) %>% 
  summarize(
    water_none_min = min(water_none, na.rm = TRUE),
    water_none_mean = mean(___, na.rm = TRUE),
    water_none_median = ___(___, na.rm = TRUE),
    water_none_stdev = sd(___, na.rm = ___),
    water_none_iqr = IQR(___, na.rm = ___),
    water_none_max = ___(___, na.rm = ___),
    sanitation_none_min = min(sanitation_none, na.rm = TRUE),
    sanitation_none_mean = mean(sanitation_none, na.rm = TRUE),
    sanitation_none_median = ___(___, na.rm = TRUE),
    sanitation_none_stdev = sd(___, na.rm = ___),
    sanitation_none_iqr = IQR(___, na.rm = ___),
    sanitation_none_max = ___(___, na.rm = ___)
  )
```

## Exercise 8 — Time series for selected entities

**Goal:** Explain the Exercise 6 turnover with a time-series plot.

Create a time-series visualization that helps you understand why the entities with the highest rates of no sanitation changed between 2000 and 2020.

- Include the entity `"World"` so that you can compare country trajectories with the global series.
- Map `Entity` to an aesthetic so that the series can be told apart.
- Try more than one `geom_` if you like (`geom_line()` is the usual starting point; points on top of lines can help).
- Comment on the rates of change in no sanitation service for at least two of the entities you plotted.

A time-series plot shows how a variable changes across years.

Choose **World**, **India** (already in the skeleton), and three other entities from your Exercise 4 and Exercise 6 lists. A useful mix is one entity that improved enough to leave the 2000 top five and one that was still near the top in 2020.

```{r country-global-changes-demo, echo = TRUE}
wat_san %>% 
  filter(Entity == "World" | Entity == "India" | Entity == "___" | Entity == "___" | Entity == "___") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = ___, y = ___, color = ___)) +
  geom_line()
```
